{{short description|Gives necessary and sufficient conditions for two braids to have equivalent closures}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[File:Alexander closure of a braid.svg|350px|thumb|Braid closure]]}}

{{Distinguish|Markov number#Markov's theorem}}

In [[mathematics]] the '''Markov theorem''' gives necessary and sufficient conditions for two [[braid (mathematics)|braids]] to have closures that are equivalent [[knot (mathematics)|knot]]s or [[link (knot theory)|link]]s. The conditions are stated in terms of the [[group (mathematics)|group]] structures on braids. 

Braids are algebraic objects described by diagrams; the relation to topology is given by [[Alexander's theorem]] which states that every [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] or [[link (knot theory)|link]] in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] is the closure of a [[braid (mathematics)|braid]]. The Markov theorem, proved by Russian mathematician [[Andrey Markov Jr.|Andrei Andreevich Markov Jr.]]<ref>A. A. Markov Jr., [http://www.mathnet.ru/links/4318fdf834b204d4d948d0f977413652/sm5359.pdf Über die freie Äquivalenz der geschlossenen Zöpfe]</ref> describes the elementary moves generating the [[equivalence relation]] on braids given by the equivalence of their closures. 

More precisely Markov's theorem can be stated as follows:<ref>{{cite book |last=Birman|author-link=Joan S. Birman|first=Joan|title=Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups|publisher=Princeton University Press|date=1974|series=Annals of Mathematics Studies|volume=82}}, Theorem 2.3 on p. 51</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Kauffman|first=Louis|author-link=Louis H. Kauffman|date=1991|title=Knots and Physics |url=|location= |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=}}, p.95</ref> given two braids represented by elements <math>\beta_n, \beta_m'</math> in the braid groups <math>B_n, B_m</math>, their closures are equivalent links if and only if <math>\beta_m'</math> can be obtained from applying to <math>\beta_n</math> a sequence of the following operations:
# [[conjugacy class|conjugating]] <math>\beta_n</math> in <math>B_n</math>; 
# replacing <math>\beta_n</math> by <math>\beta_n\sigma_{n}^{\pm 1} \in B_{n+1}</math> (here <math>\sigma_i</math> are the standard generators of the braid groups; geometrically this amounts to adding a strand to the right of the braid diagram and twisting it once with the (previously) last strand); 
# the inverse of the previous operation (if <math>\beta_n = \beta_{n-1}\sigma_{n-1}^{\pm 1}</math> with <math>\beta_{n-1} \in B_{n-1}</math> replace with <math>\beta_{n-1}</math>).

In 1974 American mathematician [[Joan Birman]] published a [[monograph]], ''[[Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups]]'', based on a graduate course she taught as a visiting professor at [[Princeton University]] in 1971–72; this book contains the first complete proof of the Markov theorem.<ref name="notices">{{cite journal|author=Margalit, Dan|author-link=Dan Margalit (mathematician)|title=The Mathematics of Joan Birman|journal= AMS Notices |volume=66|issue=3|year=2019|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201903/rnoti-p341.pdf}}</ref>
